title: How have you implemented the Page Object Model (separate test logic → page interaction methods → locators), what does it buy you (reusability, maintainability, single place to fix a changed locator), and what are its limitations and how do you avoid them (bloated page classes, duplication → extract components/fixtures/helpers)?
shortTitle: Implementing the Page Object Model, its benefits, and its limitations
keyPoints: POM separates test logic (what) from page interaction (how), with locators as hidden implementation details inside the page object
Reusability: many tests share the same page methods, so login or transfer logic is written once
Maintainability: a changed locator is fixed in one place and every spec using it is instantly corrected
Bloated page classes are the main limitation: decompose into component objects for shared UI parts like headers and date pickers
Fixtures inject ready-to-use page objects and handle setup, keeping page objects focused purely on interaction
Keep business assertions in specs, not inside page objects, so page objects stay reusable across tests expecting different outcomes

s1_definition.oneliner: The Page Object Model puts a page's locators and action methods in one class so tests express intent and a changed locator is fixed once, and you keep it healthy by extracting component objects, fixtures, and helpers to prevent bloated, duplicated page classes.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Three-way separation** – Locators inside the page object, interaction methods wrapping actions, and test logic in specs calling those methods.
- **Reusability** – Many tests share the same page methods. Login is written once and reused everywhere.
- **Maintainability** – A changed locator is fixed in exactly one place. Every spec using it is instantly corrected.
- **Readability** – Specs read as user intent: login, makeTransfer, assertBalance.
- **Limitations** – Bloated page classes and duplication. Fix by extracting component objects, fixtures, and helpers.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, instead of every test knowing the exact buttons and boxes on the transfer screen, you appoint one expert clerk, the Transfer page object, who alone knows where every control is. Tests just ask the clerk to "make a transfer." If the bank rearranges the screen, you retrain only that one clerk. The danger is one clerk responsible for an enormous screen; you fix that by giving shared parts their own specialist clerks.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Page Object Model: Three-Way Separation
  ─────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TEST SPEC (what)                │
  │  transfer.spec.ts                │
  │                                  │
  │  1. navigate()                   │
  │  2. makeTransfer('A', 'B', '5k') │
  │  3. expect(success).toBeVisible()│
  └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                 │ calls
  ┌──────────────▼───────────────────┐
  │  PAGE OBJECT (how)               │
  │  TransferPage.ts                 │
  │                                  │
  │  navigate()                      │
  │  makeTransfer(from, to, amount)  │
  │  - selectOption(fromAccount)     │
  │  - fill(toAccount)               │
  │  - fill(amount)                  │
  │  - click(transferButton)         │
  └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                 │ holds
  ┌──────────────▼───────────────────┐
  │  LOCATORS (hidden detail)        │
  │  getByLabel('From Account')      │
  │  getByLabel('To Account')        │
  │  getByRole('button', 'Transfer') │
  │  getByText('Transfer Successful')│
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  Locator changes -> fix ONE page object
  Every spec keeps working
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I implement POM as a clean three-way separation: locators inside the page object, interaction methods wrapping actions, and test logic in specs calling those methods. The spec says what, the page object says how, and the locator is a hidden implementation detail.

The benefits are reusability (many tests share the same page methods), maintainability (a changed locator is fixed in one place), and readability (specs read as user intent). The limitations are bloated page classes and duplication. I fix those by decomposing into component objects, delegating setup to fixtures, extracting shared logic into helpers or base classes, and keeping business assertions in specs so page objects stay reusable.

At the National Bank of India, when a release restyled the transfer screen, I fixed locators in one TransferPage object and every spec passed without edits. I also refactored a god page object into composed component objects, cutting its size and enabling reuse across pages.

Remember one sentence: POM separates what from how, centralizes locators for single-point maintenance, and stays healthy when you decompose into components, delegate setup to fixtures, and keep assertions in specs.
